claim: The attach path no longer puts multi-megabyte data URLs into innerHTML and prepares independent files concurrently; image/PDF encoding runs after the chip exists.
command: Playwright MCP browser_evaluate against http://localhost:4317 (the desktop UI's app.js served by the then-available browser preview server, scripts/companion-dev.mjs, removed in a separate change), calling addAttachmentFiles / prepareAttachment / attachmentsForRequest with generated File objects and the real 8 MB MP4 fixture.
model: none (local Chromium engine in the Playwright MCP browser)
machine: Apple M5 Pro, 18 CPU cores, 25.8 GB RAM, macOS 27.0.0, Node 26.8.1

fixtures.image5mb: generated 5 MB PNG (random header, incompressible body)
fixtures.pdf10mb: generated 10 MB byte stream starting with %PDF-
fixtures.text2mb: generated 2 MB plain text (rejected by the 50,000-character cap)

before.note: The 94/44/15 ms numbers were measured on the pre-change app.js with the same generated files; the 115.8/270.8 ms numbers come from the UI survey's Chromium measurement of four 7.35 MB JPEG data URLs.

after.videoPlaceholder: visible in the change handler before the frame resolves ('读取中…')

comparison: Four 5 MB images: 94 ms of serial data-URL work plus ~28 MB of innerHTML parsing removed; the chip path creates ordered blob URLs in 3 ms. Four 12 MP photos: 69 ms to prepare four 240 px thumbnails (4.9 KB each) versus 94 ms plus full-resolution decode for the old previews. Image/PDF base64 is produced in the background (3 ms / 8 ms) and awaited only if the send arrives first.
limits: Chromium numbers, not WKWebView numbers; the packaged desktop app was not profiled.
The native NSOpenPanel latency was not measured and may dominate the owner's click.
The 561 ms first video frame is unchanged; only the placeholder feedback and multi-video concurrency improve.

Server extraction was deliberately not parallelized: four real PDFs measured 273 ms sequential vs 356 ms with Promise.all; page-level concurrency throws DataCloneError; 20-page OCR measured 2.34 s sequential vs 2.10 s with four pages.
Timings are single runs with host load; treat them as approximate.
